paras: The lynching of Elias Robertson was the hanging of a nineteen-year-old Black man by a crowd of 300 to 400 people at Morgan's Fork, Franklin County, Mississippi, on or shortly before October 9, 1881. Robertson was accused of assaulting an elderly white widow, Mrs. Ellen Johnson, and the crowd, described as both Black and white, decided his fate by a vote before hanging him in daylight. Newspapers that carried the story stressed the vote and the crowd's mixed racial makeup, under headlines such as "Lynched by Popular Vote" and "The Voice of the Majority."

According to a dispatch from Vicksburg, Mrs. Johnson, a 65-year-old widow living at Morgan's Fork, was visiting a neighbor when Robertson overtook her on a lonely stretch of road. The same dispatch charged that he knocked her down with a stick, choked her, threatened to cut her throat and "outraged" her, and other versions likewise accused him of outraging and beating her.

As word spread, large crowds of men searched for Robertson until he was caught near the Jefferson County line. His captors were Black: a "colored man" in the Vicksburg account and "a party of colored men" in the Corinth version. They took him to Morgan's Fork, within half a mile of the place of the alleged assault, where he was held while the crowd gathered.

Within two hours, the Vicksburg dispatch said, 300 or 400 people "both black and white" had assembled, and after the question of what to do with him was raised, the crowd voted unanimously to hang him. He was hanged at once, in daylight on the public highway, and one brief added that he was hung to an oak limb. The dispatches reported that good order prevailed throughout and that as many as 400 people witnessed the hanging.
No account mentions an officer, an inquest, an arrest or any official response, and no follow-up report was found.

The story reached the press through two closely related versions, a Vicksburg dispatch dated October 9 printed by the Chicago Daily Tribune and a Corinth dispatch dated October 11 that ran in the New Haven Morning Journal and Courier and, as a special to the Cincinnati Times-Star, in the Memphis Public Ledger. Both versions stated the accusation as fact and used terms such as "brutish scoundrel" and "young demon" for Robertson. The Tribune called the hanging "one of the most quiet and orderly hangings," the Times-Star special opened with "A terrible retribution," and the New Haven paper headed its version "Speedy Punishment for a Ravisher."

A one-sentence item reporting that Robertson was lynched by "several hundred citizens, white and black" circulated in syndicated news columns, appearing in the Richmond Democrat in Missouri on October 13 and in the Huntsville Gazette, the Milan Exchange and the Grenada Sentinel on October 15. The item ran again in the Batesville Guard on October 19, and the Pulaski Citizen reprinted the Times-Star story on October 27, printing the name as "Ellis Roberson." The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer's brief was the only one to use the word "mob" and to mention the oak limb.

The versions differ on small details: the Tribune printed Robertson's age as "10" where the matching Corinth text reads "nineteen," and accounts give the captors as one Black man or several. Estimates of the crowd range from "300 or 400" to "not less than four hundred."

reader.title: Lynching of Elias Robertson
bases: A crowd of several hundred people assembled at Morgan's Fork, voted to hang Elias Robertson, a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman, and hanged him (A1, A2, A4, A6).

Robertson was hanged by a crowd of 300 to 400 people after a vote, with no court or officer involved, as punishment for an alleged assault on a white woman (A1, A4, A6); the papers call it a lynching (A2, A5).

The Vicksburg (A1) and Corinth (A3-A4, A6) versions share whole sentences and appear to derive from one original account, and the briefs (A2, A5) condense it; no local, independent or later report was found.

accounts.label: Vicksburg dispatch (Oct. 9)
accounts.gist: Gives the alleged assault in detail, says a colored man captured Robertson, and that 300 or 400 people voted unanimously to hang him; calls it one of the most quiet and orderly hangings.

accounts.label: Corinth dispatch / Cincinnati Times-Star special
accounts.gist: Largely the same text, with captors given as 'colored men' or 'a party of colored men' and Robertson's age as nineteen.

accounts.label: News-column briefs
accounts.gist: One-sentence or one-paragraph condensations: a young negro lynched by several hundred citizens, white and black; one adds that he was hanged to an oak limb.

framing.detail: The Vicksburg dispatch called the alleged assault a 'flendish deed', Robertson a 'brutish scoundrel' and 'young demon', and praised the hanging as quiet and orderly.

The Times-Star special ran as 'The Voice of the Majority' and opened by calling the lynching 'A terrible retribution' on 'a miserable brute'; the New Haven paper headed it 'Speedy Punishment for a Ravisher'.
Syndicated news columns ran a single neutral-toned sentence stating the accusation as fact and the lynching by 'several hundred citizens, white and black'.

conflicts.note: No version found gives 60; all briefs that give a number say 65.
The Tribune's '10' sits in the same sentence that reads 'nineteen' in A6 and is likely a printing or OCR error.
All agree the captors were Black; they differ on number.
Same order of magnitude; A1 and A6 also say the hanging was witnessed by 'as many as 400'.
